zone.name: Southern Canyons (Spencer, Lindenkohl, Poor Man's, Norfolk)

headline: Rough Monday, Green Gold by Thursday: Poor Man's Yellowfin Bail Out the Week
subhead: A short-period blow shut us down early, but squid-soaked water off Poor Man's and steady bluefin at Norfolk turned a slow start into a real week.
body_markdown:
Call it a split-decision week. Monday and Tuesday we sat at the dock watching 3 to 4 foot slop stack up on a nasty four-second period — that's wind swell, not groundswell, and it makes for a miserable ride out past the Baltimore Channel. By Wednesday afternoon it laid down enough to run, and from Thursday through the weekend Poor Man's Canyon flat-out bailed us out. If I'm grading the week, I'd call it a C-plus that finished like a B.

Here's the thing about running four canyons out of Cape May and Ocean City — you can't fall in love with one piece of water. I had three boats calling me Wednesday night asking where to point the bow, and I sent all three different directions based on what I was hearing from guys already out there. That's the whole game this time of year.

Poor Man's was the story. We worked the edge east of the tails, around 38°37'N/73°58'W, dropping down the 100-fathom curve where the water turned that milky jade-green that tells you the squid are thick underneath you. Illex and shortfin squid have been balled up out there for two weeks now, and the yellowfin are sitting right on top of them. Sizes ran the gamut — plenty of 40-to-70-pound class fish mixed with a few genuine bigeye pushing past 100 that came on the troll around daybreak. Standard spread of ballyhoo behind Green Machines and small Ilanders on the short riggers, but the real difference-maker was dropping a naked ballyhoo flat-lined off the shotgun in that green water — that's where the bigger fish were sitting. At night, guys anchored up and lit the water with underwater squid lights picked off a handful of bigeye on butterfly jigs worked slow through 200 to 300 feet. Not every boat that tried it connected, but the ones that did had a real shot at a fish over the century mark.

Norfolk, out of Ocean City, was the quiet steady producer all week — less flashy than Poor Man's but more consistent. Bluefin have been sitting on the humps in 20 to 25 fathoms working up toward the canyon edge itself, chewing on sand eels and rainbait pushed up by the same warm surface water we're seeing inshore — NY Bight buoy read 71.6°F this week, and that's roughly the flavor of water riding out over the shelf right now. We trolled small cedar plugs and green machines on the meat rig around the humps early, then shifted to jigging vertically once the sun got up and the fish went down — 200-gram speed jigs worked with a slow pump-and-wind put schoolie-class bluefin from 20 to 40 pounds in the box on three separate trips this week. Wahoo showed up as a bonus for one boat running a straight high-speed spread — 12 to 14 knots with cedar plugs and small Ilanders down the drop-off — but that was one fish, not a pattern yet. I wouldn't build a trip around wahoo at Norfolk this week, but I'd rig for the possibility.

Spencer Canyon gave us white marlin, but scattered — not the kind of week where you mark six or eight in a day. Two boats out of Cape May had multiple bites working the 50 to 60 fathom edge west of the canyon head, teasing fish up on a dredge and switching them over to naked ballyhoo on circle hooks. One boat went 3-for-5, another went 1-for-4, and a couple came home having seen fish but never converted. That's marlin fishing — you put your teasers in front of enough fish and some of them commit. Mahi showed as incidental catches around any floating structure or weed line we crossed on the way out — nothing giant, mostly schoolie-sized fish in the 5 to 12 pound range, though one boat did pull a 38-pound bull off a lobster pot buoy on a small green-and-yellow popper. Worth keeping a spinning rod rigged and ready on the run out, because you never know when you'll cross a good line.

Lindenkohl I'm giving a pass on this week. The water up there hasn't been holding the same bait concentration as Poor Man's — less squid sign, cleaner blue water instead of that jade-green tuna color — and the one report I got back was a long day for one modest yellowfin. I'd rather send a boat south to Poor Man's or Norfolk right now than gamble on Lindenkohl waking up.

Looking ahead, the forecast has southwest winds building into a heat dome pattern by midweek, which usually means calmer seas but also means watching afternoon thunderstorm cells pop off the beach — standard July stuff. If that squid stays balled up on Poor Man's, I'd keep pointing boats there first; that's historically been one of the better stretches of the season for yellowfin numbers, and the second week of July has a track record of turning it on in these canyons. Norfolk should stay steady for bluefin as long as the humps keep holding bait. My plan for next week is simple — Poor Man's at first light for yellowfin, with Norfolk as the backup if the green water moves or thins out. I'd have a naked ballyhoo rigged and ready either way.
